cim_eredeti: Is AI Going To Get Really Creative and Come For Your Job? - Walter Bradley Center for Natural and Artificial Intelligence
szoveg_eredeti:
One of the Thursday panels at COSM 2026 (November 18–20) addressed a nagging issue for artists, writers, and entrepreneurs — will AI become so creative that it puts me out of a job?

The COSM panelists thought that the question arises from a misunderstanding about what AI does. AI is a compilation of what others have done and can do. It is not what you will choose to do in the future. You might, in fact, use it to do more of your own work.

Reflecting on the ultimate origin of creativity were philosopher Jay Richards, digital artist Nathan Jacobson, attorney Casey Luskin, and computer engineering professor Robert J. Marks. We’ll be looking at each of their contributions in turn in upcoming posts. For now, some snippets.

Richards started the 11:00 am panel by offering some thoughts about the difference between humans and machines:

Jay Richards (01:46 min): I, as a philosopher, not a technologist, have been interested in this subject for 25 years. Pretty much all of the most interesting philosophical and anthropological questions converge in the technology of artificial intelligence.

But things have changed over the years. I can say when I first started thinking and writing and reading about this, honestly, in the late 1990s, there was a distinction that was super helpful: weak artificial intelligence and strong artificial intelligence.

And in fact, if you read Ray Kurzweil in the late 1990s — who’s of course an advocate of strong artificial intelligence and singulitarian and optimistic transhumanist — his views were that we are developing technologies that will at some point become intelligent in the way we are or sentient in the way we are. So I knew what he’s arguing. At some point, that terminology and distinction just dropped out completely. And we now talk, we say things like artificial general intelligence or super intelligence.

In fact, I’d say I’ve read 25 books in the last year on this subject and almost every single one essentially said, look, this is just sort of a waste of time to have this kind of conversation.

That is very helpful if you don’t want to answer the question. You just sort of presuppose it or you just don’t bring it up.

Here’s a brief snippet of each of the three panelists’ contributions. More later:

Nathan Jacobson: (10:02 min) … My daughter, when she was young, had a mirror friend. She would teach her friend in the mirror to brush her teeth, how to prepare for the day and talk with her, confusing that image in the mirror for having the kinds of qualities that she has.

But of course, none of those qualities were beheld or possessed by that mirror and the friend. And now half a decade into the AI age, it’s time for us to grow past this confusion, this illusion that these machines are doing the things that only humans can.

There’s a categorical divide here between the man and all the machines, the remarkable machines that we have made. So my final claim: the machine in the mirror is not a person.

Casey Luskin: (14:58 min) … So an LLM is basically just using numbers and vectors to predict what words should be outputted based upon the materials that it’s been trained on or ingested as they often say. But the AI can’t reason or think. It can’t look at your question and say, I really don’t know the answer to this question. What it’s going to do is it’s going to average over all the materials it’s been trained on and give you the answer that it doesn’t really think, but that it calculates is the most likely answer based upon those training materials. And it does this even if it’s giving you the wrong answer.

That’s where AI’s get hallucination comes from. So the AI is not really doing reasoning or thinking. It’s not really intelligent. It’s just averaging over a bunch of vectors and it’s going to output an answer even if the answer is not correct.

Robert J. Marks: (19:49 min) … I want to address the creativity in the sense of AI creating better AI. This is something which dystopians have said, yeah, it’s going to get better and better and better and reach the singularity and eventually take over the world.

There’s reasons why that is not going to happen. And one of the best explanations is so-called information degradation. And I’m going to show you a little bit of the math, no equations, but a little bit of the math from information theory that indicates why this cannot happen…

This happens in the game of Telephone where you used to sit around and whisper in the ear of somebody and then they whisper that message in somebody else’s ear and you go around the room and at the end you don’t get the same message which was initially transmitted…

Ray Kurzweil says, “Within a quarter century, nine biological intelligence will mask the range and subtlety of human intelligence. It will then swoop past it.” … In 1958, there was an article published in the New York Times that says the Navy has developed a new robot that it thinks will be able to eventually think, gain consciousness, reproduce, and do incredible things.

That robot is nearly seventy years late…

Stay tuned for more thoughts from this and other panels at COSM 2026: Reality Check!
